![Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

In *LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling* [[1]](#ref-1) (arXiv preprint, May 2026), [Qi Cao](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=46U_bhgAAAAJ), [Yufan Wang](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2108111686), [Peijia Qin](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=BnkNS80AAAAJ), [Shuhao Zhang](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Rj13ryoAAAAJ), and [Pengtao Xie](https://pengtaoxie.github.io/) (UCSD) propose a test-time control loop that turns pre-solve and post-solve self-assessment signals into explicit retry, stop, and aggregate decisions, lifting a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 from 48.3 to 56.9 pooled accuracy on STEM, code, and multimodal benchmarks without any parameter updates.

Two terms borrowed from cognitive psychology carry the argument:

- **Feeling of knowing (FOK)** — a *pre-solve* self-assessment. Before a single token of reasoning is generated, the model is prompted to emit a scalar in $[0,1]$ estimating how likely it is to solve the problem. Because the signal is read off before any work is done, it can be used to *gate* inference budget: low-FOK problems get more attempts, high-FOK problems get fewer.
- **Judgment of learning (JOL)** — a *post-solve* self-assessment. After producing a candidate solution, the model emits a second scalar in $[0,1]$ estimating how likely that specific answer is to be correct. Because the signal sits between solve and accept, it can be used as a *verifier* — replacing the separate critic model that self-correction loops typically need to decide when to stop.

The two scalars sit outside the answer text rather than inline with reasoning, which keeps them structurally separable from the chain of thought and cheap to elicit. Figure 1 lays out the empirical premise in three panels: (a) shows the prompting setup that elicits FOK before answering and JOL after; (b) shows that those self-reports track actual correctness — accuracy rises monotonically from low- to high-confidence bins for both signals across all candidate models; (c) shows that the same models do *not* currently allocate reasoning length according to those signals — output length is roughly flat across the low/medium/high confidence bins. Panels (b) and (c) together motivate the harness: the calibration signal exists (b), but the model isn't using it to direct effort (c). The harness in this paper is the machinery that closes the gap between (b) and (c) by turning the two scalars into routing decisions at inference time.

> Large language models (LLMs) often expose useful signals of self-monitoring: before solving a problem, they can estimate whether they are likely to succeed, and after solving it, they can judge whether their answer is likely to be correct. However, these signals are typically measured or elicited in isolation, rather than used to control inference. In this work, we ask whether LLMs possess latent metacognitive ability that can be turned into effective test-time control. Inspired by the Nelson–Narens theory from cognitive psychology, we propose a *metacognitive harness that separates monitoring from reasoning*. For each problem, the model first reports a *pre-solve feeling-of-knowing (FOK)* signal; after each solve attempt, it reports a *post-solve judgment-of-learning (JOL)* signal. Rather than treating these signals as passive confidence estimates, the harness turns them into an explicit control interface for reasoning: it decides when to trust the current solution, when to retry with compact metacognitive feedback, and when to pass multiple attempts to a final aggregator. Across text, code, and multimodal reasoning benchmarks, *our harness substantially improves a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 base model without parameter updates* or benchmark-specific fine-tuning. On the evaluated public benchmark snapshots, it *raises pooled accuracy from 48.3 to 56.9* and exceeds the strongest listed leaderboard entries on the three primary evaluation settings: HLE-Verified, LiveCodeBench v6, and R-Bench-V. These results suggest that strong LLMs may already possess useful metacognitive ability, but require an explicit control harness to act on it during reasoning.

## Method

The harness has two stages:

- ***Metacognition diagnosis*** runs once per candidate model on a 100-problem anchor set disjoint from any downstream benchmark. For each problem the model emits an FOK score (no reasoning allowed), produces a solution, and emits a JOL score. The triples $(\mathrm{FOK}_i, \mathrm{JOL}_i, y_i)$, where $y_i$ is correctness, are scored for discrimination and calibration, then used as supervision to fit a small **per-model controller**: a support vector machine over the two-dimensional feature $(\mathrm{FOK}, \mathrm{JOL})$, with isotonic post-hoc calibration, trained via GroupKFold cross-validation on the 100-question anchor set. The kernel is selected per base model (polynomial degree 3 for Sonnet-4.6, linear for Opus-4.6); the calibrated output is a joint $P(\text{correct})$ thresholded at $p_{\rm stop}=0.7$. The paper rules out a hand-crafted alternative explicitly: the best closed-form rule the authors found, $(1{-}\mathrm{JOL})\cdot\mathrm{FOK}$, underperforms the learned SVM, so raw self-reports are not directly actionable as routing signals.
- ***Deployment*** applies the fitted controller at inference. Low-FOK problems get extra reasoning budget directed at them; solutions whose post-solve $P(\text{correct})\geq p_{\rm stop}$ are accepted and no further attempts are generated; mixed cases continue drawing additional solutions from the same base model and route the set to a final aggregator.

**Training is moved off the base model, not eliminated.** The framing claim of "no parameter updates" is accurate at the LLM level — Sonnet-4.6's weights never change — but the harness still requires a small, fast supervised fit per base model on the 100-question anchor set. The cost is two orders of magnitude below conventional fine-tuning and produces an artifact (the SVM) that's a few kilobytes rather than a checkpoint, but it is training, and it has to be redone when the base model changes.

Figure 2 lays out the harness as a Nelson–Narens [[2]](#ref-2) two-level loop: a meta level monitors reasoning state through the self-reported signals, while an object level performs test-time scaling actions (retry, stop, aggregate) under meta-level supervision. The two levels are deliberately separated so that the same base model serves as both the reasoner and the monitor, with the controller — not a fine-tune — deciding when each role activates.

## Results

The harness wraps a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 base model — no fine-tuning — and is evaluated on three benchmarks chosen to span the modalities the paper cares about: HLE-Verified [[3]](#ref-3) for text reasoning, LiveCodeBench v6 [[4]](#ref-4) for code, and R-Bench-V [[5]](#ref-5) for multimodal STEM. Two comparison sets are reported:

- **Public single-model leaderboards** — top-1 entries from frontier model families on each benchmark.
- **Matched-inference-budget baselines** — four prior test-time scaling approaches under a fixed compute budget per question:
  - *Vertical scaling* (one trajectory, more reasoning per attempt): *Self-Refine* [[6]](#ref-6) and *Budget Forcing* [[7]](#ref-7).
  - *Parallel scaling* (N independent attempts combined by a separate selector): *Verifier Reranking* [[8]](#ref-8) [[9]](#ref-9) and *Aggregator* [[10]](#ref-10).

Table 1 reports both comparisons: Panel A vs. the leaderboard, Panel B vs. the test-time scaling baselines (with average attempts and dollar cost per question).

![Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="table1-full.png"}

Headline findings:

- **Pooled accuracy: 48.3 → 56.9 (+8.6)** *against same-base test-time scaling baselines (Panel B)*. Largest gain among all listed methods at the lowest cost per question among the parallel approaches.
- **Beats every public single-model leaderboard entry on the three primary settings (Panel A).** Notably +12.0 over GPT-5.2-H on HLE-Verified (52.5 → 64.5) and +19.6 over o4-mini-H on the LiveCodeBench Hard split (63.5 → 83.1).
- **Pareto-dominant on cost.** $0.78 per question vs $1.32–$1.42 for parallel-selection baselines; matches Aggregator's accuracy at 55% of its cost. The savings come from FOK gating: easy problems short-circuit at the first high-JOL solution instead of paying the full N-attempt budget.
- **Average attempts: 2.4 vs 4.0** for parallel baselines, with a higher accuracy ceiling. Effort is allocated unevenly — confident problems exit fast, uncertain problems get more attempts.
- **Ablations.** Removing any of three ingredients — calibrated decision rules from the diagnosis step, directed retry guided by JOL feedback, or per-attempt context management — drops the gain materially. Uniform sampling and longer single-trajectory reasoning, the obvious cheaper substitutes, do not recover the harness's accuracy.

![Table 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table2.png){fig-align="center"}

## My Notes

- **Closing the open loop — the contribution sits inside a multi-year arc.** [Kadavath et al.](/posts/20260504-kadavath-mostly-know/) [[11]](#ref-11) already showed in 2022 that frontier models are well-calibrated on lettered multiple choice and can self-evaluate via $P(\text{True})$ and $P(\text{IK})$ probes. What the metacognition literature has been missing is a closed-loop way to *act* on those signals during inference rather than treating them as a measurement target, exactly the gap a recent position-paper line argued for ([Liu and van der Schaar's intrinsic metacognitive learning frame](/posts/20260430-intrinsic-metacognitive-learning/) [[12]](#ref-12)). This paper is one of the first published instances of that loop actually closed end-to-end.
- **The SVM is the external verifier [Huang et al.](/posts/20260516-cannot-self-correct/) [[13]](#ref-13) said the loop needs.** Huang's ICLR 2024 result was that intrinsic self-correction fails without an external signal. [Reflexion](/posts/20260516-reflexion/) [[14]](#ref-14), framed as self-reflection, actually depends on environment reward at each retry. The metacognitive harness sits in the same family: the model's FOK and JOL scalars only correlate with correctness, and the SVM is the piece that *learns* a calibrated $P(\text{correct})$ from ground-truth labels on the 100 anchor questions. The labels are the actual external signal; the harness's distinction is supplying it offline once per model rather than at inference via an oracle or critic LLM.
- **Per-model calibration is partial credit.** [Cacioli's 33-model atlas](/posts/20260522-metacognition-atlas/) [[15]](#ref-15) shows that the same LLM's ability to know when it's wrong varies sharply across knowledge domains — best on Applied/Professional questions, worst on Formal Reasoning and Natural Science. The harness's per-model SVM is the right direction, but per-(model, domain) is where Cacioli's evidence points.
- **Portability across model families is the open question.** A separate May 2026 line of work, [The Compliance Trap](/posts/20260522-compliance-trap/) [[16]](#ref-16), shows that 8 of 11 frontier models lose up to 30.2 accuracy points under instructions that force the model to commit to a confident answer when it would otherwise hedge or abstain, with the most-capable reasoning models suffering the worst absolute collapse. Anthropic's Constitutional AI [[17]](#ref-17) shows near-perfect immunity. The harness uses Sonnet-4.6, and FOK/JOL elicitation matches compliance-forcing's shape, so the headline gain may be conditional on the alignment family rather than the harness design. A natural follow-up replicates the harness across Gemini, GPT-5, and DeepSeek bases to see whether the gain transfers, or whether Claude-specific alignment was doing the work.
